result: Goal set: read the delivered documents in order and answer later detail questions about the retellings only, ignoring unrelated documents. This will now anchor every prompt going forward.
OK

Vira Toland, born 1912 in Ostrey Hollow, recounts how a 1919 Association letter accusing the Hollow's milk of adulteration led to station tester Ansel Keddie eventually being caught skimming cream and dismissed, fracturing his family's relationship with his brother-in-law Emmet Brant for good.
This report is for the year 1966 and recommends a levy for 1967 (not 1908), so it contains no information about a 1908 road levy.

Effie Loomis, the Association's longtime secretary, gives a records-based history explaining Article VII's rule that each station's own test governs pay, and how the 1925 arbitration board paid Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 while finding "no cause established," never addressing the condemned measures crate from 1923.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie, the dismissed Ostrey Hollow tester, gives a formal denial and a detailed unsent letter describing his meticulous testing method, the unexplained 1911 anomaly when a borrowed measure raised readings to 3.80, and his bafflement at being put out despite the board finding "no cause established."
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Ansel Keddie's granddaughter Ivy Keddie presents forensic evidence to a historical society showing that undersized pipettes—not theft—caused the Ostrey Hollow station's chronic low milk-fat readings, exonerating her grandfather decades after his 1925 dismissal.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague, the Association's longtime bookkeeper, defends his ledger entries showing a steady 5.25% "station gain" between Ostrey Hollow's credited and delivered butterfat, arguing the station's one-man setup invited pilferage while insisting he flagged the pattern to manager Selby Vose back in 1916 and was told to drop it.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, presents his terse yearly circuit-book entries on Ostrey Hollow, culminating in his 1923 discovery that the station's pipettes wouldn't deliver their marked measure, leading him to condemn the whole crate and order new glass.
Lemma 2.1 is named the "Interleaving" lemma.

Curator Halbert Nym catalogs sixteen items of physical and documentary evidence—invoices, ledgers, test books, bulletins—tracing the Ostrey Hollow pipette-shortage story from 1896 through its 1958 exoneration of Ansel Keddie.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Manager Selby Vose defends the Association's $3,800 settlement and his 1919 warning circular, insisting the Ostrey Hollow tests rose in 1924 because patrons stopped watering their milk once scrutiny began, dismissing the condemned testing apparatus as mere routine wear rather than the true cause.
A sailings query spanning more than 14 days returns error code `SKF-2201`.

r09 — Roy Brant (Emmet Brant's son, Hessel Bottom farmer), 1955 account of his father's weigh-book, showing the farm's own scale always agreed with the station's weights (ruling out theft of milk quantity) while the test consistently ran 0.17 points low year-round, and detailing the 1919 rift with brother-in-law Ansel Keddie.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage for Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.

r10 — Rosalie Cudd (Alder Corners cheesemaker, daughter of founder Jerome Cudd), 1958 letter to Ivy Keddie giving her father's independently-kept test records for four Hessel Bottom farmers (steady ~3.80 across 1915–1930), corroborating that the Bottom's milk was never actually poor or watered.
The man's crown will cost $1,480 after insurance.

r11 — Professor Leland Vaught, Bulletin No. 471 introduction (1958), explaining the proportional-error mechanism of undersized pipettes and presenting the exonerating math — though this version's own numbers (5 dozen pipettes, 16.27cc mean, 0.9244 ratio, true average 3.905, 118,000 lb shortfall) conflict internally with its own closing quoted conclusion and with the figures given in other retellings (six dozen pipettes, 16.72cc, 3.80 true average, 76,000 lb).
Vermilion is the color named in the third paragraph (Bettine Rausch's apron).

r12 — Dell Rundle, schoolteacher, 1939 jubilee pamphlet (reprinted 1959) on the Association's fifty-year history, retelling the Ostrey Hollow "stolen cream" theory as valley consensus but then retracting it in a same-publication postscript after seeing the ledger's "station gain" entry — though this account uses several figures (Vose as "nephew," 44,000,000 lb intake, July 12 condemnation date, eleven surviving pipettes, $19,600 loss) that conflict with other retellings' numbers.
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words.

r13 — Alonzo Frick, arbitration board chairman, 1946 bar association recollections, describing the 1925 hearing's three competing (unproven) explanations—Vose's watering theory, Teague's insinuation of Keddie's theft, and the wet-hay theory—plus Keddie's private admission he privately suspected the patrons; this account cites the station's average as 3.16 and the patrons' claimed loss as 67,000 lb, both figures diverging from other retellings' numbers.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley.

r14 — Hobart Sill, retired buttermaker (41 years at Larrow Green), 1934 exit remarks recalling that Hollow cream consistently weighed in "heavy" versus the station's own paperwork and asserting his personal belief that Hollow patrons were watering their milk, while also revealing he supplied the station's original 1896 test glassware from his own bench before their outfit arrived.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the "Trebbin norm."

r15 — Nyle Grigg, 1919 covering letter reprinting his 1908 committee report on Ostrey Hollow, claiming vindication from Bulletin No. 214 but misstating its finding as "two tenths" (versus the bulletin's actual "five hundredths") and claiming year-round 1908 sampling that contradicts his own report's stated January–March window.
The level-27 accessor `chart.rawCells()` is removed at API level 31.

r16 — Dr. Roland Kepp, veterinary surgeon, 1926 paper to the Farm Club arguing (with Q&A appended) that Hessel Bottom's soil/mineral deficiency—not the station—explains the ~0.21-point test gap, dismissing the 1911 borrowed-measure anomaly as a mere six-week summer fluke and misquoting Bulletin No. 214's finding as "two tenths" rather than five hundredths.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.
r17 — Hazel Brant (Emmet's granddaughter, Roy's daughter), 1981 taped interview recalling the weigh book, the 1910 leaf, and Ivy's discovery that the glassware caused the shortfall.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta (the scarf worn by the woman called Tuesday).
r18 — Duncan Keddie (Ansel Keddie's son, Ivy's father), 1968/1970 family notes clarifying kinship ties and tracing the fate of each key record book.
The coroner's jury found that Obadiah Chalmers died by accidental drowning from a fall off the flume edge while working, with no evidence of another person's involvement.
r19 — The Ashlin Chronicle (unsigned newspaper feature), 3 Oct 1958, reporting Bulletin No. 471's exoneration of Ansel Keddie via Ivy Keddie's discovery of the short-delivering pipette crate.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.
r20 — Junia Ammon, firm historian of Ammon & Sons (Tarnet), 1949 chapter reproducing the 1897 pipette invoice and the firm's 1923 non-answer letter.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle.
r21 — Cleve Oram (cream hauler's son), 1977 taped recollection of the Ostrey Hollow station, the loft crate, and the 1925 hearing.
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

r22 — Orin Falke, Ordell County agricultural agent, 1959 board report synthesizing the whole Ostrey Hollow question, with an appended correction citing Bulletin No. 214's actual figures and fixing Ivy Keddie's relation to Ansel as granddaughter.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.
r23 — Bertram Kyle, retired Cooperative office clerk, 1953 memoir of the ledgers, the station accounts, and the arbitration paper trail he handled at Larrow Green.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal (the endpapers of Halvane's collected edition).
r24 — Orra Keddie (Ansel's wife, Emmet Brant's sister), diary extracts 1897–1934 covering the station's daily life, the family rift with Emmet, and Ansel's dismissal and death.
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899, was $13.88.
